title: Five years: the long story
tomorrow: a raga, a rule or a line: what changed Simran most?

lines: A TURBAN BY A FARM TRUCK.
cards: Saturday morning, and the kitchen table is covered in photographs with curled corners. Simran came in for chilies and got stuck.
Bebe holds up one: a man in a turban beside a farm truck, squinting into the Central Valley sun. Your great-grandfather, she says. He drove, like your dad drives.
Simran asks where the story starts, expecting a port, a ship, an airport. Bebe shakes her head. Kartarpur, she says.
A village on a riverbank. Start there.

teach.b: Tradition says that after years on the road, Guru Nanak settled at Kartarpur, by the Ravi river, and farmed. People came to sing with him, eat with him and work the fields.
That's the long story's first scene: not a palace, a farm with a shared kitchen.

teach.h: GURU TO GURU, TOWN TO TOWN.
teach.b: Then the light passes from Guru to Guru. Towns grow around them. Amritsar and its pool.
The Khalsa at Anandpur. And there are martyrs, people who gave their lives rather than give up their faith. Sikhs don't keep that part in a museum.
Ardas, the prayer that closes almost any Sikh gathering, remembers the Gurus, the Guru's sons, the five beloved ones and the martyrs, by name and by deed.

Then, much later in the long story, families leave Punjab: for cities, for ships, for farms half a world away, carrying the Granth with them. That's how a riverbank village reaches a California kitchen.
Now the part to tell a friend tonight.

teach.h: SARBAT DA BHALA: THE GOOD OF ALL.
teach.b: After all that remembering, Ardas ends with two wishes: chardi kala, rising spirits, and sarbat da bhala, the good of all. Not the good of Sikhs. The good of everyone.
Simran looks at the man by the truck for a long time.

how: Ardas is said standing, often with folded hands, at the close of Sikh services and at home; it remembers the Gurus, the Sahibzade, the Panj Pyare and the martyrs, and ends asking for chardi kala and sarbat da bhala, the good of all.

o: a look back at the Sikh story from Kartarpur to now
a long pilgrimage some Sikhs make to Punjab
the years Guru Nanak spent farming by the river

games.q: a classmate says, so when you pray, it's just for Sikhs, right? what can Simran honestly say about Ardas?
o: it ends asking for sarbat da bhala, the good of all, not only Sikhs.
yes, Ardas is for the Sikh community; others pray their own way.
Sikhs don't ask for anything in prayer; they only remember the Gurus.
games.why: Ardas remembers the Gurus and the martyrs, then asks; its last wish is sarbat da bhala, the good of everyone.

practice: Close your eyes. If you know Ardas, say quietly the part that remembers those who gave their lives; if not, bring to mind the names from this week's stories, one at a time, and let each one go by slowly.
End where Ardas ends: sarbat da bhala, the good of all.

wordCard.voice: Five years: the long story. From Guru Nanak's farm at Kartarpur to a kitchen table in California, remembered every day in Ardas.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: the good of all, the last wish of Ardas.

carryVoice: Your line: the long story, and it ends on the good of all. One photo is on Simran's phone now.
